text:
### Observed differences

- Six activities — A33, A35, A36, A37, A38 and A39 — each ran exactly once in essentially every case in the earlier window (participation 100 in 100 traces, no repeats); in the later window each appears in only about 47–57 in 100 traces, still at most once per case. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006]
- Entry into this block changed: earlier, about 98 in 100 of A30's outgoing transitions went to A33, A35 or A36 (roughly a third each); in the later window A30 spreads across all six activities (about 12–19 in 100 each, roughly 45 into A33/A35/A36 and 52 into A37/A38/A39), so A37, A38 and A39 now follow A30 directly, which essentially never happened earlier. [DIR001]
- Exits from A33, A35 and A36 changed accordingly: earlier, about 29–37 in 100 of their outgoing transitions led to A37, A38 or A39 and none led to A31; in the later window about 26–34 in 100 lead directly to A31 and only about 0–2 in 100 still lead to A37, A38 or A39. [DIR002, DIR003, DIR004]
- Distances shrank: earlier, A31 followed A33, A35 or A36 at 4–5 steps (within the 5-step window in about 62–67 in 100 of their traces), and A37, A38 or A39 followed A30 at 4–5 steps; in the later window both pairs sit 1–3 steps apart in nearly every case. [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG006, LAG009]
- Cross-group proximity collapsed: pairs spanning the two groups (e.g., A33–A38, A36–A39) were within five steps in about 199–200 of 200 earlier traces but in only 4–5 later traces — consistent with the groups rarely running together, though the later counts are too small for precise rates. [LAG005, LAG007, LAG008, LAG010, LAG011]
- Event positions shifted only mildly (A30 later, mean 0.62 → 0.67; A33/A35/A36 later when present, about 0.68 → 0.74; A39 and A31 slightly earlier); these are trace-relative positions, not clock times. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that the six-activity block was reorganised from two consecutive groups into two alternative groups: earlier, every case ran A30, then A33/A35/A36 in varying order, then A37/A38/A39 in varying order, then A31; in the later window A30 routes directly into one of the two groups (about 45 vs 52 in 100 cases), only the chosen group's three activities run — which is why each of the six now appears in only about half of the traces — and A31 immediately follows the A33/A35/A36 group when that group runs. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006, DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG006, LAG009]

The supporting signs are direct and mutually consistent rather than merely numerous: the new direct transitions into A31 and the direct A30→A37/A38/A39 entries are observed in the routing profiles, the shortened distances in the lag distributions, and the participation drop in the occurrence profiles; overall, 27 control-flow items qualified where fewer than one would be expected if nothing had changed, each with an empirical strength of about 0.995. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG006, LAG009, OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006]

Limitations: the aggregate windows cannot exclude that the later window mixes old-sequence cases with restructured ones; the group shares (about 47 and 56 in 100) sum to slightly more than 100, so a small share of cases containing both groups cannot be ruled out; and nothing is observed about what follows the A37/A38/A39 group or A31. [OCC001, OCC004, OCC006]

Other differences: the mild event-position shifts listed above accompany the restructuring but were not needed to infer it, and five further lag differences (A33–A38, A35–A37, A35–A38, A36–A38, A36–A39) rest on only 4–5 later-window observations each and cannot be interpreted beyond the co-proximity collapse noted above. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006, LAG005, LAG007, LAG008, LAG010, LAG011]
